analysis.one_liner: Caps domestic island shipping rates near international price indexes to lower costs for Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico and Guam.
analysis.headline: The bill to benchmark domestic shipping rates against international indexes never got a hearing or a vote — it sat in a House subcommittee until Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Shipping between the U.S. mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam and other islands is reserved by federal law for U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed ships, and rates on those routes run far above what international carriers charge for comparable distances. This bill would write a concrete standard into law: a rate in that trade would count as 'reasonable' only if it came within 10 percent of an international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission. That would give island shippers and consumers a legal handle to challenge rates that are dramatically higher than the rest of the world pays. The bill never received so much as a hearing; it was referred to a subcommittee and died there when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and businesses of Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam and other noncontiguous areas, who currently pay a shipping premium embedded in the price of virtually everything they buy — food, fuel, cars, building materials. Shippers who move goods on those routes would also gain a concrete legal standard for challenging rates.

how_it_helps.text: It defines a 'reasonable' shipping rate for noncontiguous domestic trade as one within 10 percent of a comparable international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission, replacing the vaguer current-law standard and giving shippers and island communities a concrete way to challenge high rates.

Because international ocean rates are generally far below domestic noncontiguous rates, a enforceable 10-percent benchmark would put downward pressure on the shipping surcharges baked into island prices for food, fuel, cars, and household goods.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S.-flag ocean carriers that hold the noncontiguous domestic trade, which operate under the Jones Act with higher operating costs (U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed ships) and little competition; their rates would be pulled toward much lower international benchmarks.

drawbacks.text: Ships operating in the noncontiguous domestic trade cost more to run than foreign ships — they must be U.S.-built and U.S.-crewed — so pinning rates to an international index could squeeze carriers below their actual costs, potentially reducing service frequency, ship investment, or routes to smaller islands.

The bill depends on the Federal Maritime Commission recognizing a 'comparable international ocean rate index,' and it is not obvious that such an index exists for these routes, which have no true international equivalent — making the standard hard to apply in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: families in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico and Guam pay a shipping premium on nearly everything they buy, and even partial convergence toward international rates would ease that. The cost is that the carriers' higher operating costs are genuine, and forcing rates toward an international benchmark could squeeze service frequency, investment in ships, or route viability — the strongest good-faith objection. The bill's design also has an untested piece: it relies on the Federal Maritime Commission to recognize a "comparable international ocean rate index," and it is not clear such an index exists for these unique domestic routes. Weighing that, the main problem with this bill is not that it was flawed so much as that it was never examined at all — it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before Congress ended.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee, and stayed there until the 118th Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 13, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, and no further action was ever taken.
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The U.S.-flag shipping carriers that hold the noncontiguous domestic trade are better off — they keep charging rates far above international levels, and island consumers keep paying the difference.

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to benchmark noncontiguous domestic shipping rates against international indexes.

for.name: Del. James Moylan
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor, representing Guam, another island community affected by high shipping rates.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled any action on the bill; after a single referral to the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee on April 14, 2023, the bill sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Hawaii Democrat sponsored the bill and the sole cosponsor was a Republican delegate from Guam — a bipartisan pairing of island representatives, but only two members of Congress total ever signed on.

industries.industry: Jones Act / noncontiguous domestic ocean carriers
industries.note: These U.S.-flag carriers, which face little competition on routes between the mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico and Guam, currently charge rates far above international levels. A rate benchmark tied to an international index would directly cap what they can charge, threatening their margins.

industries.industry: Island retailers, importers and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico and Guam
industries.note: Every store and importer on the islands pays the high domestic shipping rates on incoming goods. A workable rate benchmark would lower their input costs and, eventually, shelf prices.
